issues.legal_issue: An official authorized only to execute government lease documents cannot independently allot government land without authority to make the allotment.
material_facts: The land belonged to the government.
A Sub-Divisional Officer approved an allotment and executed a lease in favour of an individual, and later directed that the land be transferred to purchasers of buildings or debris on it.
The record did not establish that the Sub-Divisional Officer had authority to allot the land; the applicable government directions vested the relevant approval authority in the District Collector.
The District Collector cancelled the allotment and transfer, and the High Court upheld that decision.
issues.conclusion: The Sub-Divisional Officer lacked authority to allot the government land, so the allotment and resulting lease did not create an enforceable right to the land.
issues.legal_principle: The Rules regarding Management of Government property authorized the Sub-Divisional Officer to sign a lease deed on behalf of the Governor but did not empower that officer to allot government land. The applicable government directions vested the relevant allotment authority in the District Collector. The judgment also notes the Collector's cancellation power under Section 122(6) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Revenue Act.

predicates.challenge_to_government_land_allotment: A party challenged the validity of an allotment of government land.
predicates.government_land: The land at issue belonged to the government.
predicates.allotting_officer_lacked_allotment_autho: The official who made the allotment had no authority to allot the government land.

issues.definition: When a challenged allotment concerns government land and the allotting official lacked authority, the allotment is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A transfer of government land cannot be made merely because the transferee purchased buildings or debris from the existing grantee.
material_facts: The purchasers' registered sale deed covered constructions or debris, not the government land itself.
The purchasers applied for mutation and stated that they had purchased debris rather than the land.
The Sub-Divisional Officer directed that the land be transferred to the purchasers on payment of land revenue, without making a fresh allotment to them on the merits of their eligibility.
issues.conclusion: The sale of the buildings or debris did not authorize the Sub-Divisional Officer to transfer the government land to the purchasers; at most, a valid authority could consider their application for a grant on its merits.
issues.legal_principle: A sale of structures or debris does not convey government land. Even assuming an officer had authority to grant a lease for non-agricultural purposes, that authority would not permit transferring the land to purchasers on the basis of the sale; their eligibility for a grant would have to be considered on its merits.

predicates.government_land: The land at issue belonged to the government.
predicates.sale_conveyed_only_structures_or_debris: The purchaser acquired buildings, structures, or debris but did not acquire the government land.
predicates.land_transferred_without_merits_consider: An official transferred the government land to the purchaser without deciding whether the purchaser qualified for a fresh grant on the merits.

issues.definition: If a sale conveys only structures or debris and an official transfers the government land without considering eligibility for a fresh grant, that transfer is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A person seeking extraordinary writ relief over an asserted land grant must plead and establish the foundational facts showing a lawful grant and a resulting legal right.
material_facts: The purchasers sought relief under Article 226 of the Constitution concerning the cancellation of the allotment and transfer.
They did not plead and establish the authority under which the Sub-Divisional Officer had allotted the land to their predecessor or transferred it to them.
They failed to establish that the allotment and transfer lawfully gave them rights in the government land.
issues.conclusion: The purchasers failed to establish a lawful entitlement to the land, and the High Court properly refused to restore the Sub-Divisional Officer's order.
issues.legal_principle: A person invoking the extraordinary jurisdiction of the High Court under Article 226 must come with clean hands and make full and complete disclosure. Foundational facts must be pleaded so the court can examine the nature and basis of the alleged right, and the claimant must establish that the grant and transfer lawfully created that right.

predicates.article_226_writ_claim: A claimant sought extraordinary relief from a High Court under its constitutional writ jurisdiction.
predicates.claim_depends_on_land_grant: The claimant's asserted right to land depended on a grant or transfer of that land.
predicates.foundational_facts_not_pleaded_or_establ: The claimant did not plead or establish the facts showing that the grant or transfer was authorized and created a legal right.

issues.definition: When a writ claim to land depends on a grant and the claimant does not plead or establish the foundational facts for that grant, writ relief on the claimed land right is unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: A court may refuse to set aside an administrative order for a procedural defect when doing so would restore an earlier order that is illegal or otherwise not in accordance with law.
material_facts: The show-cause notice alleged that the Sub-Divisional Officer was not authorized to grant the land, but did not specify the earlier proceedings withdrawing that officer's powers.
The final order referred to those earlier proceedings.
The underlying allotment and transfer orders were invalid and without jurisdiction.
Setting aside the Collector's order would have restored those invalid orders.
issues.conclusion: Even if the omission in the show-cause notice amounted to a technical breach of natural justice, it did not justify interference because that would restore orders that were not in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 226, a court need not set aside an order merely because of a breach of natural justice where doing so would restore an earlier unlawful order. The Court relied on Venkateswara Rao v. Government of A.P. and M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, which recognize that discretionary writ relief may be refused in those circumstances.

rule.if: writ_review_of_administrative_order and specific_ground_omitted_from_notice and earlier_order_is_unlawful and quashing_would_restore_earlier_order

predicates.writ_review_of_administrative_order: A party asked a court to review an administrative order through its writ jurisdiction.
predicates.specific_ground_omitted_from_notice: The notice did not identify a specific ground later referred to in the final administrative order.
predicates.earlier_order_is_unlawful: The earlier order in the party's favour was illegal or otherwise not in accordance with law.
predicates.quashing_would_restore_earlier_order: Setting aside the challenged administrative order would restore the earlier order.

issues.definition: When a writ challenge concerns a notice defect but quashing the administrative order would restore an unlawful earlier order, the court may refuse to set the order aside.
